source_operations.before: [F3] Linear IVPs with continuous coefficients have unique local solutions, and their maximal solutions extend while bounded ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]], [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]).
source_operations.after: [F3] A homogeneous square-matrix IVP with continuous coefficients on a compact interval has a unique solution throughout that interval, with one-sided endpoint derivatives ([[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]). The same existence and uniqueness hold for vector initial data by putting the vector in the first column of the initial matrix and the remaining columns equal to zero.

source_operations.before: 1.1 The coefficient $A$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. For $0\le s\le t\le1$, let $U(t,s)$ be the solution operator of $v'=A(t)v$. Local existence and uniqueness follow from [F3]. For any initial vector $\xi$, [F6] and the equation give $\|U(t,s)\xi\|_2\le\|\xi\|_2+a_0\int_s^t\|U(r,s)\xi\|_2\,dr$; Gronwall [F4] yields $\|U(t,s)\|_2\le e^{a_0(t-s)}$. Thus the solution remains bounded and [F3] extends it through $t=1$. In particular $U$ exists on the full triangle $0\le s\le t\le1$. [given, F3, F4, F6]
source_operations.after: 1.1 The coefficient $A$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. For $0\le s<1$, apply [F3] on $[s,1]$ with initial matrix $I$ at $s$; its solution is the homogeneous solution operator $U(t,s)$ throughout that interval. Put $U(1,1)=I$. For any initial vector $\xi$, [F6] and the equation give $\|U(t,s)\xi\|_2\le\|\xi\|_2+a_0\int_s^t\|U(r,s)\xi\|_2\,dr$; Gronwall [F4] yields $\|U(t,s)\|_2\le e^{a_0(t-s)}$ for every $0\le s\le t\le1$. The full interval of existence comes from [F3], not from boundedness alone. [given, F3, F4, F6]

source_operations.before: 2.2 For data $(g,q)\in Z$, let $p$ be the unique solution of $p'=Ap+g$, $p(0)=0$. Local existence and uniqueness follow from [F3]. Since $p'$ is continuous, [F6] gives $\|p(t)\|_2=\|\int_0^t p'(s)\,ds\|_2\le\int_0^t\|p'(s)\|_2\,ds$. Pointwise, $\|p'(s)\|_2\le a_0\|p(s)\|_2+\|g\|_\infty$, so monotonicity in [F6] gives $\|p(t)\|_2\le\|g\|_\infty+a_0\int_0^t\|p(s)\|_2\,ds$, hence $\|p\|_\infty\le E\|g\|_\infty$ by [F4]. This bound extends $p$ through the full interval by [F3]. Every solution with initial value $\xi$ equals $U(t,0)\xi+p(t)$, since their difference solves the homogeneous linear IVP with initial value $\xi$ and uniqueness [F3] applies. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]
source_operations.after: 2.2 For data $(g,q)\in Z$, form the continuous $(d+2)\times(d+2)$ coefficient $H(t)=\begin{bmatrix}A(t)&g(t)\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ on $[0,1]$. Apply [F3] with initial matrix whose first column is $(0,1)^T\in\mathbb R^{d+1}\times\mathbb R$ and whose remaining columns are zero. The last component of its first solution column has derivative zero and initial value one, hence is identically one by [F6]. Its upper component $p$ therefore solves $p'=Ap+g$, $p(0)=0$ throughout $[0,1]$. Any other such $p$ gives the same matrix solution by placing $(p,1)^T$ in the first column and zeros elsewhere, so uniqueness in [F3] proves uniqueness of $p$. Since $p'$ is continuous, [F6] gives $\|p(t)\|_2=\|\int_0^t p'(s)\,ds\|_2\le\int_0^t\|p'(s)\|_2\,ds$. Pointwise, $\|p'(s)\|_2\le a_0\|p(s)\|_2+\|g\|_\infty$, so monotonicity in [F6] gives $\|p(t)\|_2\le\|g\|_\infty+a_0\int_0^t\|p(s)\|_2\,ds$, hence $\|p\|_\infty\le E\|g\|_\infty$ by [F4]. Every solution with initial value $\xi$ equals $U(t,0)\xi+p(t)$, since their difference solves the homogeneous linear IVP with initial value $\xi$ and uniqueness [F3] applies. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra, construct]
